tier_reason: kostya/benchmarks is a public third-party suite: benchmark code json/json-java/src/main/java/bench/TestJava.java vs json/test_nlohmann_json.cpp, json/test_libjson.cpp and json/test_boost_ptree.cpp, C++ flags in common/commands.mk (-O3 -march=native -flto=auto, g++ 16.1.0, clang++ 22.1.8), Java build in json/json-java/Makefile, CPU Intel Xeon E-2324G in the README Environment section. Every number in the record matches the README Json table rows (UPDATE: 2026-07-19).

corrections.baseline: nlohmann/json (C++), json-c (C library called from a C++ driver) and Boost.PropertyTree (C++) as built by kostya/benchmarks; DSL-JSON does NOT beat RapidJSON (all variants incl. SAX Precise), Boost.JSON, simdjson, yyjson, yajl, gason or DAW JSON Link in the same table
corrections.claimed_speedup: Time in seconds (lower is better), from the kostya/benchmarks README Json table (median of runs, UPDATE: 2026-07-19): Java (DSL-JSON) 0.571; C++/clang++ (Nlohmann) 1.182; C++/g++ (Nlohmann) 1.266; C++/clang++ (json-c) 1.185; C++/g++ (json-c) 1.187; C++/clang++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.589; C++/g++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.907. That is about 2.1-2.2x faster than Nlohmann and json-c, 4.5-5.1x faster than Boost.PropertyTree (derived from page data). In the same table it is slower than C++/g++ (simdjson On-Demand) 0.060, C++/clang++ (DAW JSON Link NoCheck) 0.070, C++/clang++ (simdjson DOM) 0.103, C++/g++ (gason) 0.127, C/gcc (yyjson) 0.131, C++/g++ (RapidJSON) 0.154, C/gcc (yajl) 0.362, C++/g++ (Boost.JSON) 0.374 and C++/clang++ (RapidJSON SAX Precise) 0.500.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++ built with g++ 16.1.0 (-std=c++23) and clang++ 22.1.8 (-std=c++23 -stdlib=libc++), both with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk); nlohmann/json is a depth-1 git clone of HEAD (version not pinned) used as the single header; json-c is the Debian libjson-c-dev package linked with -ljson-c, so the json-c library itself is a distribution build, not compiled with the suite's -O3 -march=native flags. Java side: DSL-JSON 2.0.2 (json/json-java/Maven.list, fetched with coursier) compiled by json/json-java/Makefile with plain 'javac -proc:full' (annotation processor generates the converter; the --release 26 flag of common/commands.mk JAVAC_BUILD is not used by this test), run as 'java -cp <fat jar> bench.TestJava' with no JVM flags (HotSpot defaults). The README Environment table lists Java 24.0.2, while the current docker/Dockerfile pins JDK 26.0.1, so the exact JDK of the 2026-07-19 run is ambiguous.
corrections.caveats: Beats only the slow C/C++ JSON libraries; the fast ones (simdjson, DAW JSON Link, gason, yyjson, RapidJSON, yajl, Boost.JSON, RapidJSON SAX Precise) are about 1.1-9.5x faster than it in the same table (derived from page data), so this is not Java beating the C/C++ incumbent for fast JSON. Work is not identical: the Java test deserialises straight into generated Root/Coordinate classes that declare only coordinates and x, y, z (name, opts and info are skipped, not materialised) with JsonReader.DoublePrecision.LOW (reduced number-parsing accuracy), while the nlohmann test builds a full DOM (std::map objects, std::string keys and values) and calls get<double>. The C++ timed window also includes destruction of the nlohmann DOM when calc returns, whereas Java leaves its objects to the GC; the json-c driver never frees its tree. JIT warm-up is not separated: the self-test calls calc twice on tiny inputs, so the timed run is a single cold-ish parse (this hurts Java, not the baselines). Results are printed but not cross-checked between languages. json-c is a Debian prebuilt library. The README says implementations are written 'as the average software developer would write them'. The DSL-JSON README cites this benchmark only as 'fastest performing Java JSON library' and makes no C++ comparison; its FAQ explanation of speed is the library author's own. JDK version ambiguous (README table Java 24.0.2, Dockerfile JDK 26.0.1).
corrections.why_faster: Not a language win (same_algorithm false). From the benchmark sources: DSL-JSON binds directly into two generated classes through an annotation-processor converter, skips unneeded fields, uses low-precision double parsing and allocates no DOM, while nlohmann/json allocates a std::map node and std::string per key and value and frees the whole DOM inside the timed window. The DSL-JSON README FAQ adds: almost zero allocations, byte-level work, better byte[]-to-type conversion algorithms, minimized unexpected branching and compile-time databinding instead of reflection.

notes: Numbers verified row by row on the kostya/benchmarks README; tier A holds. Main shortcomings: wins only over slow DOM libraries (Nlohmann, json-c, Boost.PropertyTree), loses to every fast C/C++ parser incl. yajl; schema binding with skipped fields and low-precision doubles against a full DOM whose teardown is timed, so the gain is library design, not Java. Corrected the Java build description (json-java/Makefile uses plain javac -proc:full) and flagged the JDK version ambiguity.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: same public suite and methodology as the DSL-JSON record (benchmark code json/test.jl vs json/test_nlohmann_json.cpp, json/test_libjson.cpp, json/test_boost_ptree.cpp; Julia v1.11.6 run with --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no per README and common/commands.mk; C++ flags in common/commands.mk; CPU Intel Xeon E-2324G). A missing mechanism is not a tier criterion, and the mechanism is readable in the JSON3 sources (tape-based reader).

corrections.baseline: nlohmann/json (C++), json-c (C library called from a C++ driver) and Boost.PropertyTree (C++) as built by kostya/benchmarks; JSON3 does NOT beat RapidJSON (all variants), Boost.JSON, simdjson, yyjson, yajl, gason or DAW JSON Link in the same table
corrections.claimed_speedup: Time in seconds (lower is better), kostya/benchmarks README Json table (median of runs, UPDATE: 2026-07-19): Julia (JSON3) 0.700; C++/clang++ (Nlohmann) 1.182; C++/g++ (Nlohmann) 1.266; C++/clang++ (json-c) 1.185; C++/g++ (json-c) 1.187; C++/clang++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.589; C++/g++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.907. About 1.7-1.8x faster than Nlohmann and json-c, 3.7-4.2x faster than Boost.PropertyTree (derived from page data). Slower than C++/g++ (RapidJSON) 0.154, C/gcc (yajl) 0.362, C++/g++ (Boost.JSON) 0.374, C++/clang++ (RapidJSON SAX Precise) 0.500 and Java (DSL-JSON) 0.571.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++ built with g++ 16.1.0 (-std=c++23) and clang++ 22.1.8 (-std=c++23 -stdlib=libc++), both with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk); nlohmann/json is a depth-1 git clone of HEAD (version not pinned); json-c is the Debian libjson-c-dev package (distribution build, not compiled with the suite's flags). Julia side: README Environment table lists Julia v1.11.6 (the current docker/Dockerfile pins julia-1.12.6, so the exact version is ambiguous), run as 'julia --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no' (common/commands.mk JULIA_RUN); json/test.jl installs JSON3 with Pkg.add at run time, so the JSON3 version is not pinned (presumably 1.14.3, the last release before the 2026-07-19 update; not stated).
corrections.caveats: Beats only the slow C/C++ libraries; the fast ones are about 1.4-11.7x faster in the same table, yajl and Boost.JSON included (derived from page data). Work is not the same: JSON3.read fills one flat Vector{UInt64} tape (numbers parsed eagerly with Parsers.jl, strings left as offsets into the input buffer, no per-node objects), while the nlohmann test builds a full DOM of std::map nodes and std::string copies and destroys it inside the timed window; the json-c driver never frees its tree. The Julia loop is type-unstable (x = y = z = 0 starts as Int; coord["x"] returns Any), which handicaps Julia. Self-test calls calc twice on tiny inputs before timing, so most JIT compilation is outside the window but not explicitly separated. Results are printed, not cross-checked between languages. JSON3 version unpinned (Pkg.add) and Julia version ambiguous (README v1.11.6, Dockerfile 1.12.6). Package deprecated in favour of JSON.jl v1 (README notice, commit 2025-10-10), which this suite did not measure; the JSON3 README only says it is 'for speed and slick struct mapping'.
corrections.why_faster: Not a language win (same_algorithm false). From the JSON3 sources (src/read.jl, src/JSON3.jl): JSON3.read writes the parse into a single preallocated UInt64 tape, with JSON3.Object and JSON3.Array as views over that tape, so it makes no per-node heap allocations and copies no strings; nlohmann/json allocates a std::map node and std::string per key and string value and frees the DOM inside the timed window.

notes: Numbers verified on the kostya/benchmarks README; tier raised C to A for consistency with the DSL-JSON record from the same table (code, compilers, flags and CPU all public). Main shortcomings: beats only slow DOM libraries, loses to every fast C/C++ parser incl. yajl; lazy tape against a full nlohmann DOM whose teardown is timed, so the gain is library design; package deprecated, JSON3 and Julia versions not pinned. If the orchestrator prefers to keep deprecated-package entries capped, record that as a shortcoming rather than a tier cap.

tier_reason: README states the FFI implementation is 'both faster, safer, and more complete than the Lua C API of the ngx_lua module' with no numbers, benchmark code or links; one web search found only qualitative restatements (api7.ai learning-center article, a vendor of an OpenResty-based gateway, snippet only, no timings).

corrections.caveats: Qualitative claim only: no benchmark in the README and none found elsewhere (one web search turned up package mirrors and an api7.ai explainer without timings, snippet only). 855 stars, under the 1k notability guideline, kept for project notability (loaded by default since OpenResty 1.15.8.1). Not Lua beating C: the FFI path still calls C functions exported by lua-nginx-module (e.g. ngx_http_lua_ffi_shdict_get declared via ffi.cdef in lib/resty/core/shdict.lua); the gain is that LuaJIT traces are not aborted by Lua C API calls, so it is a JIT-versus-interpreter effect rather than JIT code beating AOT C. The README's own caveat: 'If the user Lua code is not JIT compiled, then use of this library may lead to performance drop in interpreted mode.' License text in the README is the two-clause BSD text (SPDX id inferred). No hardware, versions or flags.
corrections.why_faster: README: ngx_lua's default API 'is based on the standard Lua C API, which will never be JIT compiled and the user Lua code is always interpreted (slowly)', while the FFI-based API 'can work with LuaJIT's JIT compiler'; both paths end in C code inside lua-nginx-module.

notes: Tier D confirmed; metadata matches (855 stars, 288 forks, last commit 2026-08-24, BSD two-clause text in README). Kept rather than rejected per wave policy despite tier D under 1k stars. Main shortcomings: no numbers; the FFI API still calls C functions, so the win is trace-compilation of the calling Lua code, not Lua beating C; slower in interpreted mode per its own README; arguably off-category for runtime-jit-beats-aot.
